papers.abstract: Lateral cavernous-sinus extension and suprasellar tumor-arachnoid anatomy are distinct but overlapping dimensions of pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (PitNET) surgery. We evaluated whether reader-concordant preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) descriptors of these two axes show different associations with extent of resection and intraoperative cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage. In this single-center retrospective study, two blinded neurosurgeons independently assessed preoperative MRI of 53 patients: modified Knosp grade, suprasellar height, bowing index, infundibular deviation angle, and a study-specific tumor-arachnoid cleft grade. Exploratory analyses examined resection extent and Esposito-graded leakage (15 events), with post hoc adjustment for maximal tumor diameter. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) were 0.995-0.999 for continuous measures; cleft agreement was 53/53 and Knosp exact agreement 96.2%. Knosp grade was most strongly associated with non-total resection (area under the curve [AUC] 0.908; diameter-adjusted odds ratio [OR] 10.8 per SD, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.4-48.9) but not leakage (AUC 0.648). Suprasellar height (AUC 0.747) and cleft grade (AUC 0.740) showed stronger leakage associations; none of 16 patients with a wide cleft (> 2 mm) leaked. Cleft grade and height were strongly collinear (ρ=-0.81); the cleft-leakage association persisted after diameter adjustment (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.19-0.93). Lateral and suprasellar MRI descriptors, concordant between two readers, showed different, partly overlapping operative associations. Modified Knosp grade related most strongly to resection, whereas suprasellar features, particularly the study-specific cleft grade, showed stronger exploratory associations with intraoperative leakage. The cleft finding is hypothesis-generating and requires prospective external validation; added value over height and the sellar barrier is unproven.

papers.abstract: Glioblastoma frequently progresses beyond surgical margins, yet whether preoperative imaging can predict its direction remains unclear. Given the anatomical characteristics of the temporal lobe and the potential role of anterior temporal lobectomy, we evaluated FLAIR, isotropic diffusion (DTI-p), and diffusion anisotropy (DTI-q) as imaging biomarkers of directional progression after complete resection. We retrospectively analyzed a prospectively recruited multicenter cohort of patients with newly diagnosed IDH-wildtype glioblastoma confined to the temporal lobe who underwent complete resection of contrast-enhancing tumor and had preoperative diffusion tensor imaging and follow-up MRI demonstrating progression. Progression was visually classified relative to the resection cavity. Direction-specific accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were calculated, with paired comparisons using exact McNemar tests and Holm correction across all comparisons. Times to progression and death were summarized descriptively. Thirty-two patients met inclusion criteria. DTI-q demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy across all progression directions (median, 75%), compared with DTI-p (median, 50%) and FLAIR (median, 44%). DTI-q significantly outperformed FLAIR and DTI-p for lateral, superior, and inferior progression after Holm correction. Combined imaging models did not improve predictive performance over DTI-q alone. Preoperative DTI-q predicted directional progression after complete resection more accurately than FLAIR or DTI-p, supporting DTI-q as a potential imaging biomarker for spatially informed surgical planning.

papers.abstract: Robot-assisted radical cystectomy (RARC) is increasingly prevalent. However, real-world data on its mid-term effectiveness in diverse patient populations remain limited. We conducted a retrospective multicenter study of patients undergoing RARC for bladder cancer at 32 Chinese institutions (2012-2021). Baseline, perioperative, pathological, and survival data were collected. Missing data were handled by multiple imputation. Primary outcomes were overall survival (OS), recurrence-free survival (RFS), and cancer-specific survival (CSS). Multivariable Cox regression was used to identify independent prognostic factors. Among the 4395 enrolled patients, the median age was 65 years, and 85.1% were male. With a median follow-up of 26.6 months (interquartile range 12.7-47.6), the estimated 3-year OS, RFS, and CSS were 78.7%, 74.9%, and 81.7%, respectively. Multivariable analysis identified non-organ-confined disease (pT3-4) and lymph node metastasis as independent prognostic factors for worse OS, RFS, and CSS (all p<0.001). Adjuvant therapy was independently associated with worse RFS (hazard ratio 1.687; 95% confidence interval 1.389-2.049, p<0.001), and cutaneous ureterostomy was associated with worse RFS than ileal conduit (hazard ratio 1.241; 95% confidence interval 1.007-1.531, p=0.040). This large real-world study demonstrates that RARC provides satisfactory mid-term oncologic outcomes. Charlson Comorbidity Index, tumor stage, lymph node status, and urinary diversion choice significantly affect survival. These findings support the continued adoption of RARC and highlight the importance of patient selection and comprehensive perioperative management.

papers.abstract: Effective therapy remains lacking for patients with advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) whose disease progressed after standard treatment. Izalontamab brengitecan, an epidermal growth factor receptor and human epidermal growth factor receptor 3 bispecific antibody-drug conjugate with a topoisomerase I inhibitor, Ed-04, has shown clinical activity in ESCC in a phase 1b study. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of izalontamab brengitecan compared with chemotherapy in patients with advanced ESCC who progressed after first-line programmed cell death 1 protein (PD-1)/programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitor plus platinum-containing chemotherapy. This phase 3, open-label, randomized clinical trial was conducted across 80 hospitals in China. Patients with recurrent or metastatic ESCC that had progressed with first-line PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor plus platinum-containing chemotherapy were enrolled. Between March 19, 2024, and August 1, 2025 (final follow-up, October 17, 2025), a total of 704 patients were screened, and 497 were enrolled and randomized. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either izalontamab brengitecan (n = 249; 2.5 mg/kg on days 1 and 8 every 3 weeks) or physician-selected chemotherapy (n = 248; irinotecan, paclitaxel, or docetaxel) every 3 weeks. The dual primary end points were progression-free survival (PFS) assessed by blinded independent central review according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 and overall survival (OS). Of 497 patients who underwent randomization (median age, 61.0 years [range, 34-76]; 448 male patients [90.1%]), 493 received study treatment. At this interim analysis, izalontamab brengitecan demonstrated statistically significant improvement in both PFS and OS. Median PFS by blinded independent central review was 4.17 months (95% CI, 3.61-4.53 months) with izalontamab brengitecan vs 1.97 months (95% CI, 1.61-2.73 months) with chemotherapy (hazard ratio, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.40-0.63; log-rank P < .001). Median OS was 9.79 months (95% CI, 7.89-11.01 months) with izalontamab brengitecan vs 7.20 months (95% CI, 6.18-7.82 months) with chemotherapy (hazard ratio, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.48-0.82; log-rank P < .001). Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 212 of 249 patients (85.1%) with izalontamab brengitecan and 147 of 248 patients (59.3%) with chemotherapy and were predominantly hematologic. Izalontamab brengitecan significantly improved PFS and OS vs chemotherapy in patients with recurrent or metastatic ESCC whose disease had progressed after first-line treatment. These findings support izalontamab brengitecan as a new second-line treatment for this population in China. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06304974.

papers.abstract: Oral nutritional supplementation (ONS), providing supplementary oral nutrition in addition to usual food, is widely used during concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), but its optimal timing and cost utility remain uncertain. To evaluate efficacy and explore cost utility of early ONS in patients with NPC undergoing CCRT. This multicenter, open-label, randomized clinical trial was conducted at 6 Chinese tertiary hospitals from July 2021 to May 2025. Eligible patients were aged 18 to 70 years with newly diagnosed stage II to IVA NPC, a Patient-Generated Subjective Global Assessment (PG-SGA) score of 0 to 8, and planned CCRT. Key exclusions included oral intake less than 60% of requirements for 3 days or longer, inability or unwillingness to receive concurrent chemotherapy, and inability to receive oral or enteral nutrition. Data were analyzed from November 2025 to March 2026. Participants were randomized 1:1 to early ONS at CCRT start or routine ONS after prespecified nutritional decline. The primary end point was the incidence of more than 5% weight loss from baseline to CCRT completion. Secondary end points included PG-SGA score, the incidence of grade 3 or higher radiation-induced oral mucositis (RIOM), quality of life (European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire Core 30), and radiotherapy interruption. Cost utility measures included total cost, utility, and incremental cost utility ratio. Of 242 patients screened, 236 patients were randomized, and the prespecified modified intention-to-treat population included 216 patients (mean [SD] age, 46.62 [11.19] years; 168 [77.8%] male), with 107 receiving early ONS and 109 receiving routine ONS. More than 5% weight loss occurred in 70 participants (65.4% ) in the early ONS group, compared with 88 participants (80.7%) in the routine ONS group (relative risk [RR], 0.81; 95% CI, 0.68-0.96; P = .01). An intention-to-treat analysis including all randomized participants yielded a similar estimate (RR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.65-0.93). In the modified intention-to-treat population, grade 3 or higher RIOM occurred in 15 participants (14.0%) in the early ONS group vs 29 participants (26.6%) in the routine ONS group (RR, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.30-0.93). Best-case costs were $9560.56 in the early ONS group vs $9685.23 in the routine ONS group, with quality-adjusted life-years of 0.1144 vs 0.1132, respectively. This randomized clinical trial found that early ONS reduced clinically meaningful weight loss during CCRT; exploratory analyses suggested potential benefits for severe RIOM and a potentially favorable short-term economic profile. papers.abstract: Despite multimodal treatment, recurrence remains common in patients with resectable locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Whether perioperative chemoimmunotherapy improves long-term outcomes remains uncertain. To estimate the effect of perioperative camrelizumab plus chemotherapy on event-free survival (EFS) compared with standard surgery-based treatment in patients with resectable locally advanced HNSCC. The CAMORAL trial was a multicenter, phase 2 randomized clinical trial conducted at 4 academic hospitals in China between October 2020 and March 2024, with data cutoff on April 11, 2025. Patients aged 18 to 75 years with untreated, resectable stage III to IVB HNSCC were assigned to neoadjuvant-adjuvant treatment or control. Analyses used the intention-to-treat population. Data were analyzed from May 2025 to February 2026. Patients were randomized (1:1) to receive two 21-day cycles of neoadjuvant camrelizumab, 200 mg, plus albumin-bound paclitaxel and carboplatin followed by surgery, risk-adapted adjuvant therapy, and maintenance camrelizumab for up to 15 cycles; or upfront surgery followed by standard risk-adapted adjuvant therapy. The primary end point was 2-year EFS. Secondary end points included major pathological response (MPR), pathological complete response (pCR), overall survival, 2-year distant metastasis-free survival, 2-year locoregional recurrence-free survival, and safety. Of 125 included patients, 99 (79.2%) were male, and the mean (SD) age was 56.3 (11.7) years. A total of 63 patients were assigned to the neoadjuvant-adjuvant group and 62 to the control group; the median (IQR) follow-up was 24.6 (16.8-36.5) months. A total of 103 (82.4%) had oral cavity primary tumors. Among 125 patients, the 2-year EFS rate was 77.8% (95% CI, 63.6-87.0) in the neoadjuvant-adjuvant group compared with 46.1% (95% CI, 31.3-59.6) in the control group (hazard ratio, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.17-0.68; P = .001). MPR and pCR were 47.6% (95% CI, 34.9-60.6) and 25.4% (95% CI, 15.3-37.9), respectively, in the neoadjuvant-adjuvant group, with no MPR or pCR events in the control group. The 2-year overall survival rates were 92.0% and 69.1%, respectively (hazard ratio, 0.25; 95% CI, 0.10-0.64); the hazard ratio of 2-year distant metastasis-free survival was 0.15 (95% CI, 0.03-0.68). Grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 50 of 63 patients (79.4%) in the neoadjuvant-adjuvant group and 35 of 62 patients (56.5%) in the control group; 1 fatal treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in the control group. In this phase 2 randomized clinical trial, perioperative camrelizumab plus chemotherapy significantly improved EFS with manageable toxic effects, supporting evaluation of intensified perioperative immune priming in resectable HNSCC. papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This retrospective study aimed to identify molecular predictors of treatment response and survival in 207 newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients treated with Venetoclax combined with hypomethylating agents (VEN‐HMAs). After one treatment course, the composite complete remission (CR/CRi) rate was 69.6% (144/207), with 70.5% (93/132) of responders achieving minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity. According to the 2017 ELN risk stratification, the CR/CRi rates in the favorable‐, intermediate‐, and high‐risk groups were 77.2%, 64.0%, and 66.6%, respectively. For treatment response, RUNX1‐RUNX1T1 , FLT3‐ITD , and TP53 mutations independently predicted unfavorable to VEN‐HMAs therapy. Multivariable analysis identified NRAS and PTPN11 mutations as independent adverse prognostic factors for overall survival, while achievement of CR/CRi after the first treatment course and receiving hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) were favorable predictors. Based on molecular status, patients were stratified into three prognostic groups. The median OS was 9.5 months in the TP53 ‐mutant (low‐benefit) group and 21 months in the medium‐benefit group ( TP53 wild‐type with FLT3‐ITD or K / NRAS mutations). The high‐benefit group (wild‐type TP53 , no FLT3‐ITD , and wild‐type K / NRAS ) had a significantly superior OS (not reached) compared to the others ( p < 0.001), while OS between the medium‐ and low‐benefit groups was comparable ( p = 0.096). VEN‐HMAs therapy is associated with high response rates in this real‐world cohort, though treatment response varies substantially by molecular profile. A comprehensive understanding of these influencing factors and the development of refined risk stratification systems require further investigation.

papers.abstract: Abstract Adult glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive brain tumor that has yet to benefit from advances in immunotherapy. Prior studies report contrasting leukocyte immunophenotypes between tumors and an association between myeloid macrophage infiltration and worse patient outcomes. IL-8, a cytokine with both inflammatory and suppressive roles, was recently associated with M2 macrophage phenotypes in GBM. These observations raise key questions: do GBM macrophages suppress or support other immune cells, is IL-8 in GBM a mechanistic driver of GBM macrophage function, and can IL-8 instruct macrophages in situ within tumors? Here, functional experiments with primary human GBM tumor cells from initial surgical resections showed that IL-8 from GBM contributes to and is sufficient to instruct monocyte-derived macrophages that suppress healthy T cells. Notably, IL-8 protein expression was enriched in aggressive tumors contacting the V-SVZ region and was not associated with increased infiltration of cells expressing the IL-8 receptors CXCR1/CXCR2. Suppressor cells instructed by GBM ex vivo phenotypically matched myeloid macrophages observed in vivo, and neutralizing IL-8 during instruction blocked this and restored T cell proliferation. Analysis of IL-8 RNA showed the cytokine is primarily produced by CD45- tumor cells. These results suggest a model where ongoing IL-8 production by GBM cells maintains an immunosuppressive microenvironment by signaling to myeloid macrophages within the tumor. Immunotherapies relying on T cells should now investigate whether IL-8 blockade prevents instruction of macrophages into tumor-protective suppressor cells.

papers.abstract: Abstract Natural killer (NK) cells offer a promising off-the-shelf platform for cancer immunotherapy, yet their clinical efficacy is often limited by tumor-intrinsic resistance. Here, we show that loss of core microRNA (miRNA) machinery components, Argonaute‑2 (AGO2) or Ankyrin Repeat Domain 52 (ANKRD52), renders tumor cells hypersensitive to NK cell-mediated killing in both co-culture and xenograft models. Mechanistically, genetic ablation of Ago2 or Ankrd52 impairs miRNA-mediated silencing of critical mitochondrial apoptotic regulators and NK-cell-associated ligands in tumor cells, exemplified by the disrupted repression of pro-apoptotic Bim transcripts by miR-24 and miR-29b, thereby unleashing rapid TNF-α-driven apoptosis. Additionally, metabolic and ultrastructural analyses demonstrate collapsed membrane potential, diminished ATP levels, and fragmented mitochondria in Ago2- or Ankrd52-mutant tumor cells, accompanied by a lower apoptotic threshold upon TNF-α or NK cell challenge. Genome‑wide CRISPR library screen further revealed a selective fitness dependency on mitochondrial electron‑transport and ATP‑synthase genes in mutant tumor cells. Collectively, these findings define defective miRNA machinery as a tumor‑intrinsic vulnerability that couples mitochondrial fragility with increased NK-mediated cytotoxicity, nominate miRNA‑pathway status as a predictive biomarker, and propose that co‑targeting mitochondrial metabolism or apoptosis may potentiate NK‑cell therapies.

papers.abstract: Early detection of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is hindered by a lack of noninvasive biomarkers for precancerous lesions. Here, we report a circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) methylation approach for early esophageal neoplasia detection. In prospective community screening, the assay achieved standardized sensitivity of 78% at 79% specificity for the clinically actionable endpoint of high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia (HGIN) or ESCC, with stage-specific sensitivities of 76% for HGIN and 86% for ESCC. Genome-wide methylation profiling reveals HGIN as an early epigenetic reprogramming stage. Integrative spatial and single-cell RNA sequencing reveals pronounced remodeling of the endothelial-proximal epithelial cell population, whose methylation signatures are detected in cfDNA. Guided by these findings, we develop an 11-gene cfDNA methylation panel that shows robust discrimination of early-stage ESCC across three retrospective case-control sets and an independent screening-derived case-control set. Together, these results demonstrate that our cfDNA methylation panel has promising utility for early ESCC detection.

papers.abstract: Many tumors remain poorly responsive to immune checkpoint blockade. The metabolic microenvironment in tumors can mediate immunosuppression by failing to sustain productive cytotoxic lymphocyte function. Here, we showed that a coordinated ketogenic-fasting (KF) regimen sensitized immune-refractory tumors to PD-1 blockade by integrating distinct metabolic and microbial effects of ketogenic diet (KD) and intermittent fasting (IF). The KF combination established a distinct immunometabolic state that could not be fully recapitulated by either KD or IF intervention alone. KF induced systemic glucose restriction while preserving intratumoral glutamine availability and selectively upregulating the glutamine transporters SLC38A1 and SLC38A2 in tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells and NK cells, fueling interferon-STAT1 signaling and effector activity. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis identified KF-associated cytotoxic lymphocyte states characterized by enhanced nutrient access signatures, increased effector function, and reduced terminal dysfunction. Microbiota depletion attenuated KF-mediated tumor control without abolishing intratumoral glutamine enrichment. Fecal microbiota transfer and monocolonization identified Odoribacter splanchnicus as sufficient to restore tumor control and cytotoxic T-cell activity in microbiota-depleted hosts. Mechanistically, O. splanchnicus was linked to host polyamine remodeling and indole-3-lactic acid, which supported durable CD8+ T-cell functions distinct from the glutamine-driven effector arm. KF enhanced anti-PD-1 efficacy in immune-cold tumor models, and public human datasets showed concordant associations between glutamine context, Odoribacter abundance, and immunotherapy response. Together, these findings identify a diet-responsive host-microbiota metabolic mechanism that stimulates antitumor immunity and sensitizes immune-cold tumors to immunotherapy.

papers.abstract: Automated classification of glioblastoma (IDH-wt, WHO CNS Gr.4) histopathologic sub-regions in whole slide images (WSI) is essential for quantitative tumor characterization, but faces substantial challenges from intra-tumoral heterogeneity and inter-observer annotation variability. The AI-RANO & RANO-Pathology working groups organized BraTS-Path 2024, representing the first international benchmarking environment and publicly available spatially annotated dataset, towards promoting the development and fair evaluation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models to classify specific sub-regions: cellular tumor, pseudopalisading necrosis (PN), microvascular proliferation, geographic necrosis, infiltration into the cortex, and white matter penetration (WM). Multi-institutional H&E-stained WSIs had reference standard samples generated by eight expert neuropathologists, following a rigorous peer review protocol, resulting in 309,118 data samples (training/validation/hold-out testing: 96,485/62,387/150,246). Quantitative performance evaluation of six AI approaches was conducted based on multiple metrics, including Accuracy and Matthew's correlation coefficient (MCC). A robust statistically-aware ranking strategy offered statistical significance of the final rankings. Top-performing approaches employed common strategies, including large pre-trained models, ensembling, and extensive data augmentation, reporting Accuracy=0.69 and MCC=0.58. Key challenges included severe class imbalance, hampering minority class performance, and inter-annotator variability, especially for ambiguous sub-regions such as PN or WM. BraTS-Path represents a valuable public resource for glioblastoma histopathologic sub-region assessment. Our findings indicate the specific task remaining an open research problem, highlighting the influence of rare sub-regions, the absence of a consistent "gold standard" annotation protocol, and the potential of foundation models to improve generalization, guiding future research toward developing more reliable AI tools for quantitative neuropathology.

papers.abstract: The present study compared the effects of high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) with automated volume guarantee (HFOV-VG) versus careful manual high-frequency tidal volume (VThf) monitoring (HFOV-VM) on the incidences of hypo/hypercarbia in neonates. In this open-labeled, parallel-group randomized controlled trial, 60 neonates failing conventional mechanical ventilation were allocated to receive HFOV-VG (n = 30) versus HFOV-VM (n = 30) as a rescue mode. The primary outcome was the incidence of hypo/hypercarbia at 1 h. Secondary outcomes were incidences of hypo/hypercarbia at 6/12/24/48 h and beyond, time-specific trends for partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2), delivered VThf and mean airway pressure (MAP), cerebral blood flow (CBF) in the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and regional cerebral oxygenation (CrSO2), duration of respiratory support, and incidences of in-hospital adverse events. Stata 18 was used for an intention-to-treat analysis. The incidence of hypo- or hypercarbia at 1 h of intervention was 15/30 (50%) in the HFOV-VG and 13/30 (43%) in the HFOV-VM groups (p = 0.61). There was no difference in the incidence of hypo/hypercarbia with HFOV-VG versus HFOV-VM at 1 h and throughout the duration of ventilation with a similar rate of complications when used as a rescue therapy. papers.abstract: Background: Pancreatic cancer is a highly lethal malignancy. We therefore aimed to compare RNA concentration, purity, integrity, and laboratory-assigned pre-assay quality control (QC) classifications between paired fresh-frozen (FF) and formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy (EUS-FNB) specimens from solid pancreatic lesions. Methods: We evaluated 36 pairs of FF and FFPE EUS-FNB specimens for RNA concentration, absorbance ratios, RNA quality numbers (RQNs), and pre-assay QC classifications. FF tissues were placed in RNAlater-containing tubes, snap-frozen and transported in liquid nitrogen before storage in an ultra-low-temperature freezer at −80 °C at the biobank, whereas FFPE specimens were processed and stored according to routine institutional protocols. QC classifications were assigned by the analytical laboratory based on RNA measurements, electropherograms, and estimated assay input requirements. Results: FF specimens had significantly higher RNA concentrations, A260/A280 and A260/A230 ratios, and RQNs than paired FFPE specimens (all p < 0.001). No specimens achieved “Pass” status. All 36 FF specimens were classified as “Hold,” whereas 25 of 36 FFPE specimens (69.4%) were classified as “Fail” (p < 0.001). Archival storage duration was significantly longer in the FFPE “Fail” group than in the “Hold” group (median, 5.52 versus 4.14 months; p = 0.006). Conclusions: The FF workflow yielded significantly superior RNA quality metrics and fewer pre-assay QC failures than the FFPE workflow. Placement of specimens in tubes prefilled with RNAlater, followed by snap-freezing and storage at −80 °C, may offer a practical strategy for banking small pancreatic EUS-FNB specimens. However, as pre-assay QC does not guarantee downstream assay success, further validation of profiling performance and long-term stability is warranted.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: The da Vinci SP system offers a single-port configuration with flexible, multijointed instruments, but evidence comparing it with the Xi system in robotic bilateral total thyroidectomy (BTT) remains limited. This study compared surgical outcomes and postoperative complications between the two platforms. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 548 consecutive patients with thyroid cancer who underwent robotic BTT by a single surgeon between 2010 and 2024. Patients were analyzed separately according to central compartment neck dissection (CCND) or modified radical neck dissection (MRND). Propensity score matching was performed at a 1:1 ratio based on age, sex, body mass index, and tumor size. Serial calcium and parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels were additionally examined in matched patients who developed transient hypocalcemia. Results: The overall cohort included 396 patients in the Xi group and 152 in the SP group. Overall complications (34.3% vs. 21.7%, p = 0.003) and transient hypocalcemia (28.3% vs. 14.5%, p = 0.001) were less frequent in the SP group. Propensity score matching yielded 70 pairs in the CCND cohort and 47 pairs in the MRND cohort. In the matched CCND cohort, the SP group had lower rates of overall complications (18.6% vs. 40.0%, p = 0.024) and transient hypocalcemia (10.0% vs. 30.0%, p = 0.013). Complication rates did not differ significantly between the platforms in the matched MRND cohort. Surgical and pathological outcomes were generally comparable. Among patients with transient hypocalcemia, the decline in calcium at 6 months was smaller in the SP group in the CCND cohort (p = 0.013), whereas the MRND cohort showed smaller declines in PTH at selected postoperative time points but no significant between-group differences in calcium changes. Conclusion: Robotic BTT using the da Vinci SP system and the Double Bipolar Method was safe and feasible. Compared with the Xi system, this approach achieved generally comparable surgical and pathological outcomes and was associated with fewer postoperative complications in the matched CCND cohort.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Genomic profiling has become central to understanding prognosis in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), yet the canonical drivers KRAS, TP53, SMAD4, and CDKN2A do not fully explain survival heterogeneity, and the prognostic impact of co-occurring alterations remains incompletely characterized. Methods: We performed integrated genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, phosphoproteomic, and immune deconvolution analyses of publicly available PDAC datasets. Un-supervised clustering of survival extremes in MSK-IMPACT identified a subgroup enriched for concurrent TP53 and ARID1A mutations. Results: ARID1A was mutated in 7–8% of tumors across cohorts, of which 66–72% were TP53 co-mutated. Co-mutated tumors had the shortest overall survival of any subgroup (median 21.4 vs. 34.8 months in non-co-mutated tumors; log-rank p < 0.001), a pattern that persisted in the full MSK-IMPACT cohort and in independent multi-cohort validation. Transcriptomic analysis showed enrichment of MYC target, EMT, and E2F/cell-cycle programs alongside coordinated suppression of oxidative phosphorylation and lipid metabolism, with EMT tracking more closely with ARID1A mutation and cell-cycle programs with TP53 mutation. Immune deconvolution identified reduced plasma cell infiltration in co-mutated tumors. Proteomic profiling recapitulated EMT, hypoxia, and TNF-α/NF-κB enrichment, and kinase-substrate enrichment analysis inferred increased mTOR and MEK1 activity. Conclusions: These findings are hypothesis-generating and suggest that TP53 + ARID1A co-mutated PDAC represents a prognostically distinct subtype, with candidate therapeutic vulnerabilities in MAPK, mTOR, and proteostasis pathways that warrant validation in larger cohorts and functional studies.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Although local treatment has been increasingly applied to oligometastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), it remains unclear whether radiologically defined oligometastatic disease identifies patients who benefit from local treatment. We evaluated the survival impact of local treatment according to recurrence burden after curative resection of PDAC. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed patients who developed isolated liver or lung recurrence after curative-intent resection for PDAC between 2012 and 2021. Overall survival (OS) was compared according to metastatic organ, metastatic burden, and treatment strategy. Results: Among 269 patients (194 with liver and 75 with lung recurrences), those with lung recurrence, including those with oligometastatic disease, had significantly longer OS than those with liver recurrence. Although oligometastatic recurrence was associated with more favorable survival than multiple recurrences, no significant association between local treatment and longer OS was observed in either the liver or lung oligometastatic group in the conventional analysis. In patients with solitary lung recurrence, local treatment was associated with longer OS in the conventional analysis, but this association did not reach statistical significance in the time-dependent Cox analysis. Conclusions: Radiologically defined oligometastatic recurrence was associated with a favorable prognosis but was insufficient to identify patients likely to benefit from local treatment. Although an association between local treatment and longer survival was observed in patients with solitary lung recurrence, this finding was not statistically significant in the time-dependent Cox analysis and requires further validation.

papers.abstract: Background: Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in women. CCRT is standard for LACC, but its efficacy varies. This study was designed to evaluate the prognostic value of PIV in predicting short-term efficacy and long-term survival in LACC patients receiving CCRT. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 205 patients with stage IB3–IVA cervical cancer treated with CCRT at the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University (2018–2024). Variables included age, histopathological subtype, FIGO stage, lymph node status, pre-treatment serum SCCA, platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio [PLR], neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio [NLR], albumin-to-fibrinogen ratio [AFR], and PIV (calculated as neutrophil × platelet × monocyte counts/lymphocyte count). Short-term efficacy was assessed by the complete response rate (CRR) at 6 months post-treatment. Long-term survival was assessed by overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). Results: Multivariate logistic regression identified tumor size ≥ 4 cm, NLR ≥ 3.32, and PIV ≥ 350.15 as independent risk factors for poor short-term response. Multivariate Cox analysis revealed that tumor size ≥ 4 cm, FIGO stage IVA, SCCA ≥ 1.84 ng/mL, and PIV ≥ 350.15 were independent adverse prognostic factors for OS. For PFS, independent predictors included moderate/poor differentiation, FIGO stage IVA, SCCA ≥ 1.84 ng/mL, and PIV ≥ 350.15. Adding PIV to a clinical model (FIGO stage + SCCA) improved the prediction of OS. Conclusions: PIV provides independent prognostic information and may serve as a practical tool for risk stratification and personalized treatment in LACC.

papers.abstract: Objective: Development of second primary cancers (SPCs) is a significant risk for head and neck cancer (HNC) patients. This study investigates the impact of synchronous and metachronous SPCs on treatment strategies of newly diagnosed HNC. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed patients referred for curative-intent radiotherapy between 2022 and 2024. The primary outcome was the impact of SPCs on HNC (chemo)radiotherapy strategies, with SPC prevalence and distribution as secondary outcomes. Results: A total of 285 patients were included. In 28.4% an SPC was observed. A total of 8.4% had a synchronous malignancy, 16.5% were treated for another malignancy in the past and 3.5% presented with both a synchronous and metachronous cancer. The treatment was impacted in 37.0% of patients with an SPC. Treatment modifications included altered radiotherapy field (23.5%), treatment delays (13.6%), adjusted radio- or chemotherapy regimens (2.5% each), and transition to palliative care (1.2%). Conclusion: A substantial proportion of SPCs influenced the radiotherapy (RT) management in all domains. The complexity of treatment was further increased by the need for additional pre-treatment evaluations and consideration of prior therapies.

papers.abstract: Background: 177Lu-PSMA-617 radioligand treatment represents a major advancement in the management of metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), but key questions remain about tumor cell dynamics and evolution in patients who have received this drug. Here, we used a circulating tumor cell (CTC) capture assay to assess the prognostic value of CTC subsets defined by PSMA and EpCAM, and their dynamics, during 177Lu-PSMA-617 treatment in a cohort of mCRPC patients. Methods: Using a deep learning-based holographic imaging platform combined with in-flow protein marker analysis, we prospectively analyzed serial CTC samples from patients receiving 177Lu-PSMA-617 therapy at pre-treatment and on-treatment time points (n = 39 of 100 enrolled patients). PSMA and EpCAM expression on CTCs was determined by immunofluorescence staining. Proportions and absolute counts of CTC subsets delineated by PSMA and EpCAM expression were assessed in PSA50 responders (n = 19) and non-responders (n = 20). Within-patient changes in CTC subsets were compared using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Associations of CTC subset abundance and dynamics with overall survival were assessed using landmark Kaplan–Meier estimates (time zero at on-treatment sample collection) with log-rank tests and univariable Cox proportional hazards models. Results: PSMA and EpCAM expression defined three CTC subsets: PSMA+/EpCAM+, PSMA+/EpCAM−, and PSMA−/EpCAM+. The mean proportion of PSMA−/EpCAM+ CTCs increased following 177Lu-PSMA-617 in both PSA50 responders (6.2% to 18.7%; p = 0.041) and non-responders (7.9% to 15.4%; p = 0.023). This corresponded to a decrease in the proportion of PSMA+/EpCAM− CTCs, whereas the proportion of PSMA+/EpCAM+ CTCs did not decline. PSMA+ CTCs remained detectable in on-treatment samples from 37/39 patients, including 17/19 PSA50 responders. Pre-treatment counts of >5 CTCs, relative to ≤5 CTCs, were associated with shorter overall survival in the PSMA+/EpCAM+ subset (HR 3.66, 95%CI 1.35–9.94, p = 0.011), with a similar but nonsignificant trend in the PSMA+/EpCAM− subset (HR 7.00, 95%CI 0.94–51.9, p = 0.057), whereas on-treatment counts were not significantly associated with survival. Finally, on-treatment declines in PSMA+/EpCAM+ (HR 0.852, p = 0.731) and PSMA+/EpCAM− (HR 0.66, p = 0.305) CTC subsets were not significantly associated with overall survival relative to sustained high levels of these cells. Conclusions: In mCRPC patients receiving 177Lu-PSMA-617, PSMA+ CTCs frequently persist during treatment, and the pre-treatment abundance of PSMA+ CTC subsets may have prognostic value. These exploratory findings warrant validation in larger cohorts.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: A reliable preoperative estimate of World Health Organization (WHO) grade 2–3 meningiomas could complement existing criteria when planning surgery and follow-up. We assessed whether perfusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) parameters differ between grade 1 and grade 2–3 meningiomas. Methods: PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched to 6 October 2026 (OSF registration 10.17605/OSF.IO/G3Q9M). Standardised mean differences (Hedges’ g) of dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC), dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) or arterial spin labelling (ASL) parameters were pooled with random-effects models, separately for intratumoral and peritumoral measurements. Risk of bias was assessed with the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool and certainty with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. Results: Ten studies (509 patients; 129 with grade 2–3 tumours) were included. Intratumoral relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) showed no clear difference between grades (seven studies; g 0.13, 95% CI −0.71 to 0.98; p = 0.71, I2 = 84%, τ2 = 0.69). Peritumoral perfusion was higher around grade 2–3 tumours in all four studies that measured it, but the exploratory pooled estimate was imprecise (g 2.32, 95% CI −0.02 to 4.66, p = 0.051, I2 = 93%, τ2 = 2.03). Diagnostic accuracy could not be pooled. Certainty of evidence was very low. Conclusions: Current evidence does not show that intratumoral rCBV distinguishes meningioma grades. Higher peritumoral perfusion in grade 2–3 tumours, which may partly reflect peritumoral oedema, is a hypothesis to be tested in prospective studies using the 2021 WHO classification and pre-specified thresholds.

papers.abstract: Background: Cancer treatment intent sets expectations and influences treatment intensity for patients with cancer and oncology clinicians. It is not known what probability-of-cure threshold oncology clinicians use when considering a treatment to have a curative intent. The objective of this study was to determine the lowest probability of cure needed for solid tumor and hematologic oncology clinicians to consider cancer treatment curative in intent. Methods: This study was part of a cross-sectional survey of oncology clinicians (physicians and advanced practice providers [APPs]) at a comprehensive cancer center in the United States. Participants answered the question, “What is the lowest probability of cure for you to consider a cancer treatment to be of curative intent?” by providing a whole-number percentage between 0% and 100%. Results: The overall survey response rate was 66% (245 of 369 eligible clinicians), with 195 (80%) participants completing the curative intent question. Most responders were aged ≤49 years (n=137; 70.3%), female (n=124; 63.6%), and physicians (n=98; 50.3%). Solid tumor oncology clinicians reported a median probability of cure of 35% (IQR, 20%–75%), while hematologic oncology clinicians reported a median probability of 34% (IQR, 20%–70%) ( P =.90). Physicians across both specialties reported a lower probability of cure necessary for treatment to be considered curative in intent than APPs (median, 20% [IQR, 10%–40%] vs 50% [IQR, 30%–80%]; P <.001). Multivariable regression analysis showed that APPs (odds ratio, 2.88; P <.001) and clinicians of Asian race (odds ratio, 1.83; P =.01) were independently associated with a higher probability of cure required for treatment to be considered curative in intent. Conclusions: Our study revealed high variability in how clinicians dichotomize probability of cure into cancer treatment intent, with a significant discrepancy between APPs and physicians. This level of heterogeneity highlights the need to have consistent communication and appropriate expectation setting for patients, caregivers, and other health care professionals.

papers.abstract: The APOBEC3 family of cytidine deaminases, originally evolved for antiviral defense, functions as a potent source of somatic mutations in human malignancies. Although the genomic footprints of APOBEC3 were deciphered over a decade ago with characteristic mutational signatures (single-base substitution [SBS]2 and SBS13), their clinical significance is only now becoming apparent, shifting from a descriptive hallmark of mutagenesis to a potential predictor of therapy outcomes. Emerging evidence from landmark studies reveals that apolipoprotein B mRNA editing enzyme, catalytic polypeptide-like (APOBEC)-associated mutational signatures are associated with acquired resistance to targeted therapies and are an emerging biomarker of response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Mechanistically, therapy-induced activation of APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B drives the evolution of drug-tolerant persister cells and generates genomic diversity from which resistant clones emerge-a phenomenon demonstrated across epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor resistance in lung cancer, endocrine therapy resistance in breast cancer, and androgen receptor blockade resistance in prostate cancer. Concurrently, studies have shown that APOBEC mutational signatures are associated with ICI benefit, including in tumor mutational burden-adjusted analyses, most notably in urothelial carcinoma and non-small-cell lung cancer. In this study, we review this emerging paradigm, focusing on the newly established mechanisms and clinical findings. We further address the translational hurdles of detecting APOBEC mutational signatures in clinical practice and emerging therapeutic strategies, including oligonucleotide-based inhibitors and synthetic lethality. Finally, we discuss standardizing APOBEC mutational signature detection for clinical use, including developing liquid biopsy-based dynamic monitoring, and designing prospective trials with APOBEC mutational signature-based stratification.

papers.abstract: BCR::ABL1 is the oncogenic driver of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and Philadelphia chromosome-positive (Ph + ) acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), with BCR::ABL1 p210 and p190 being the predominant isoforms. Asciminib, an inhibitor that specifically targets the ABL myristate pocket (STAMP), has demonstrated efficacy in both pre-clinical and clinical studies against p210-driven CML, including cases where resistance mediated by ATP-pocket mutations has developed during prior tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy. The resistant mutation profile of asciminib is currently considered largely distinct from that of ATP-competitive TKIs. In our study, we demonstrate that several ATP-pocket mutations, including the V299L, F311I, T315I, and F317C/L, confer high levels of resistance to asciminib in the p190 isoform (> 1000-fold increase in LD50asciminib values compared to non-mutated BCR::ABL1 p190), but remain sensitive when occurring in the p210 isoform. The T315A was the only tested mutation in BCR::ABL1 p190 sensitive to asciminib. Furthermore, cells expressing BCR::ABL1 p190 mutations exhibited decreased kinase inhibition following STAMP treatment, indicative of an active kinase. Analogous results were obtained for MK-4208 (formerly known as TERN-701), a clinically active investigational STAMP compound. In the BCR::ABL1 p190 setting, this work reveals an overlapping resistance profile between STAMP compounds and TKIs, with important considerations for STAMP-based therapy. It challenges two key assumptions: that asciminib dose escalation can overcome resistant ATP-pocket mutations and that targeted therapy sensitivity profiles are equivalent between the p190 and p210 isoforms.

papers.abstract: Reactivation of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is a validated therapeutic strategy for sickle cell disease (SCD) and β-thalassemia. Cereblon (CRBN)-dependent molecular-glue degraders of HbF repressors are advancing clinically, but all share an immunomodulatory imide drug (IMiD) backbone and its class liabilities. We show that SH6, a non-IMiD small-molecule degrader, consistently induces HbF in erythroid cell lines, primary healthy-donor, SCD, and β-thalassemia CD34⁺-derived erythroid cells, and humanized NBSGW mice, at nanomolar to low-micromolar concentrations. When all compounds were tested at a matched 0.25µM concentration, HbF induction by SH6 was comparable to that of decitabine and greater than that of hydroxyurea, pomalidomide or thalidomide. HbF induction is CRBN/proteasome-dependent and associated with simultaneous degradation of the γ-globin repressors ZBTB7A and BCL11A. These findings provide proof of concept for IMiD-independent pharmacologic HbF reactivation and support further study of SH6 as a mechanistically distinct tool compound.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Objective Accurate preoperative evaluation of tumor extension in olfactory neuroblastoma (ONB) is critical for optimizing surgical planning, particularly for predicting unexpected intracranial and contralateral invasion. However, discrepancies between preoperative imaging and postoperative pathology remain a challenge. This study compares preoperative imaging with detailed pathological evaluation of anatomically oriented specimens to assess ONB progression, characterize patterns associated with unexpected invasion, and improve surgical strategies. Methods This retrospective study analyzed 58 ONB patients who underwent endoscopic transnasal resection at Jikei University Hospital between January 2018 and March 2024. Preoperative computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging were reviewed by a radiology specialist and compared with postoperative pathological evaluation of anatomically oriented resected specimens. Tumors were classified using Kadish staging and Hyams grading. Results The cohort had a median age of 53 years (range, 29–85 years), with 67.2% male participants. Preoperative staging classified 37.9% of the cases as Kadish C. Among 36 cases preoperatively staged as Kadish A or B, eight (22.2%) exhibited occult intracranial involvement. Unexpected contralateral invasion was observed in five cases, all Kadish C, frequently associated with tumor progression through bony transition areas at the skull base and nasal septum junction. Tumor invasion into the crista galli was identified in six cases, with one case suggesting metastatic spread rather than direct invasion. Conclusions Occult intracranial involvement in Kadish A and B cases may warrant consideration of skull base resection even in early stages. Contralateral invasion was limited to Kadish C and may support consideration of bilateral skull base resection in selected cases where preoperative imaging demonstrates intracranial extension and tumor proximity to key skull base transition areas. Preserving crista galli integrity during resection facilitates detailed pathological evaluation and may contribute to more accurate staging and prognostic assessment.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Gastrointestinal (GI) follicular lymphoma (FL) is a rare disease, accounting for less than 5% of GI non‐Hodgkin's lymphomas (NHL). We conducted a multi‐institutional study to clarify baseline features, common practices, and survival outcomes in primary GI FL. Methods We performed a retrospective analysis of patients with primary GI FL from 8 North American institutions. Progression‐free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and progression of disease at 24 months (POD24) were assessed. Results Two hundred and two patients were included in the analysis. Median follow up was 5.6 years. Median age at diagnosis was 60 years (range: 51–68) with a 1:1 male to female ratio. For those observed, median time to first treatment was 4.5 years. For those treated, overall response rate was 93% ( n = 112) and median time to second‐line treatment was 3.9 years. Patients who were initially observed had similar OS to those who were treated up‐front. Age ≥ 60, histologic Grade 3A, and hemoglobin < 12 g/dL at diagnosis were independent predictors of inferior survival. Based on these results, we created the GI‐FLIPI score, a prognostic index using these three readily available clinical factors to help predict outcomes in patients with GI FL. Median OS was significantly shorter in the high‐risk group compared to intermediate‐ and low‐risk groups, with a c‐index of 0.767. Conclusions This multi‐institutional analysis describes characteristics of a large cohort of patients with GI FL. The GI‐FLIPI score shows promise with high prediction accuracy and may help guide management in the future.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Breast neuroendocrine neoplasms (Br‐NENs) are rare breast tumors with substantial clinicopathological heterogeneity. The prognostic implications of the 2019 World Health Organization (WHO) classification remain incompletely characterized. This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic significance of true breast neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs) and invasive ductal carcinoma with neuroendocrine differentiation (IDC‐NE) under the 2019 WHO framework. Methods We retrospectively analyzed a pathology‐reviewed single‐center cohort of 123 patients, of whom 121 were included in survival analyses, and a separate population‐based cohort of 498 patients from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database. Institutional cases were reassessed according to the 2019 WHO criteria, whereas SEER tumor groups were defined using registry‐reported International Classification of Diseases for Oncology, Third Edition (ICD‐O‐3) morphology codes. Survival outcomes were compared using Kaplan–Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards models. Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess robustness, while exploratory propensity score matching (PSM) analyses compared IDC‐NE with conventional invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC). Results In the single‐center cohort, true NENs showed more aggressive clinicopathological features and were associated with poorer survival than IDC‐NE. In the SEER cohort, 498 patients were included, comprising 323 with registry‐defined NEN and 175 with registry‐defined IDC‐NE. NEN showed more aggressive characteristics, including a higher rate of distant metastasis at diagnosis. After adjustment for age, stage, year of diagnosis, and race, registry‐defined NEN was independently associated with worse overall survival (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.62, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.14–2.32) and breast cancer‐specific survival (HR = 2.00, 95% CI 1.30–3.06). Sensitivity analyses yielded consistent results. Conclusion Breast NENs were associated with poorer outcomes than IDC‐NE in the pathology‐reviewed cohort. The SEER analysis provided complementary population‐based prognostic evidence for registry‐defined tumor groups. Exploratory PSM analyses did not identify a statistically significant survival difference between IDC‐NE and conventional IDC.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT It is conspicuously difficult to experimentally induce cancer in embryos, especially during organogenesis. Based on this, and a number of other aspects of tumorigenesis during intra‐uterine life, it has been hypothesized that there are factors present during embryogenesis that actively suppress the development of malignancy. In this paper we review the current evidence for this. We also review data on the effects of embryonic tissue extracts on cancer cells in vitro and in vivo, and discuss potential therapeutic implications.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Venetoclax‐based regimens (VEN) have been widely adopted as frontline therapeutic options for elderly patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). However, comprehensive real‐world comparisons of VEN with conventional intensive or reduced‐intensity chemotherapy remain limited. Methods In this multicenter retrospective study, we evaluated treatment patterns and outcomes in 1370 patients with newly diagnosed AML. Patients were classified into three cohorts according to their frontline treatment: intensive chemotherapy (IC), reduced‐intensity chemotherapy (rIC), or VEN. Analyses were performed in both the overall cohort and elderly patients (aged ≥ 60 years), including baseline comparisons, uni‐ and multivariable analyses, and subgroup analyses. Results Baseline characteristics differed substantially among treatment cohorts; patients treated with VEN were older and had a higher prevalence of adverse‐risk disease than those receiving IC or rIC . In the overall cohort, VEN achieved an overall response rate ( ORR ) comparable to IC and higher than rIC (74.3% vs. 60.2%, p = 0.034). Among elderly patients, VEN was associated with a higher ORR than rIC (75.7% vs. 50.5%, p = 0.001), and the favorable ORR findings remained significant after correction for multiple testing. VEN was also associated with a lower 60‐day early‐death rate than rIC in elderly patients (1.4% vs. 20.0%, p < 0.001), suggesting better early treatment tolerability. Median event‐free survival was longer with VEN than with rIC in the primary elderly cohort analysis (9.6 vs. 6.6 months, p = 0.031), and this difference persisted in a sensitivity analysis censoring at allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, although it was attenuated in landmark and propensity‐score‐based sensitivity analyses. Overall survival did not differ significantly between the two cohorts (15.9 vs. 11.0 months, p = 0.102). Conclusion The higher response rate and lower early mortality with VEN were the most consistent findings, whereas comparative survival outcomes were considered supportive but exploratory.

papers.abstract: Postoperative hypotension can be caused by vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, severe hypovolemia, and obstruction. We sought to estimate the effects of these causes on the incidence of hypotension after major vascular surgery. We conducted a single-centre prospective cohort study of male and female adult patients undergoing major vascular surgery. We conducted point-of-care ultrasound and sidestream darkfield microscopy imaging to detect vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, severe hypovolemia, and obstruction. The primary outcome was hypotension (systolic blood pressure < 90 mm Hg or a vasopressor infusion) within 24 hr of surgery. We recruited 100 patients, of whom 89 had data available for analysis. Hypotension occurred in 20 participants (23%), vasodilation in 30 (34%), and myocardial dysfunction in 11 (12%). Severe hypovolemia and obstruction were not observed. The adjusted marginal risk difference of hypotension was 33% (95% confidence interval [CI], 14% to 53%; P < 0.001) for vasodilation and 41% (95% CI, 3% to 79%; P = 0.03) for myocardial dysfunction. Vasodilation increased the risk of intensive care unit admission by 27% (95% CI, 8% to 45%; P = 0.006) and of requiring a vasopressor infusion by 22% (95% CI, 4% to 39%; P = 0.02). Vasodilation and myocardial dysfunction increased the risk of postoperative hypotension, providing insight into the mechanistic development of postoperative hypotension. The absence of severe hypovolemia was surprising. Clinicians should assess for vasodilation and myocardial dysfunction as potential preludes to postoperative hypotension, potentially using point-of-care echocardiography and sidestream darkfield microscopy.

papers.abstract: ARDS comprises distinct inflammatory subphenotypes, including hyper- and hypo-inflammatory forms. Whether these differ in ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch and response to ventilatory strategies remains unclear. Dual-energy CT enables regional assessment of aeration and perfusion. This experimental study aimed to compare V/Q mismatch between hyper- and hypo-inflammatory subphenotypes, and respective responses to PEEP and prone positioning. In 10 pigs, hypo-inflammatory ARDS was induced by lung lavage followed by injurious ventilation. Hyper-inflammatory ARDS was produced by i.v. endotoxin infusion and fluid loading. Pigs were randomised to hypo- or hyperinflammatory ARDS, with similar oxygenation impairment. Dual-energy CT scans were obtained at individualised low, optimal, and high PEEP settings, in supine and prone positions. V/Q was derived from regional gas and blood volume and classified as low ( 2). Linear mixed-effects models included injury group, PEEP, and posture as fixed effects, and subject as a random effect. Hyper-inflammatory injury showed more severe V/Q mismatch than hypo-inflammatory injury (normal V/Q: 35% [sd=10] vs 51% [8] at low PEEP, supine position; P<0.01). Both PEEP optimisation and prone positioning improved V/Q. Prone positioning reduced high V/Q and dead space in hypo-inflammatory injury (group×posture interaction: F1,50=4.32, P=0.04), whereas PEEP reduced low V/Q and shunt in the supine position independent of ARDS subphenotype. In porcine models of hyper- and hypo-inflammatory ARDS, hyper-inflammatory injury was associated with more severe V/Q mismatch despite similar oxygenation. Distinct responses to PEEP and prone positioning support a subphenotype-tailored approach to ventilatory management.

papers.abstract: Canada faces mounting anesthesia workforce pressures, particularly in rural and smaller urban centres. Understanding residents' motivations regarding practice setting, research, and fellowship training is essential for workforce planning. We aimed to update a 2015 national survey to characterize current preferences and temporal shifts among Canadian anesthesiology residents. We conducted an anonymous, cross-sectional survey of residents in accredited Canadian anesthesiology programs (November-December 2024) using Research Electronic Data Capture. Items addressed demographics, practice setting, research experience and intentions, and fellowship plans. Selected responses were compared with 2015 survey items using Chi square tests and odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals; all tests used an alpha of 0.05. Ninety-four residents responded (12% response rate). Most preferred academic practice (63%), and half preferred to remain at their training institution (49%). Interest in rural practice was reported by 49%. Although research participation was common during medical school (94%) and residency (83%), only 18% intended to pursue research after residency. Approximately 63% intended to pursue fellowship training. Compared with the 2015 survey, there were significant increases in intention to remain at the same institution (from 35% to 50%; P = 0.02) and residency research participation (from 69% to 83%; P < 0.01), whereas intention to pursue research after residency declined (from 34% to 18%; P < 0.01). Canadian anesthesiology residents continue to favour academic practice and fellowship training, yet fewer plan to integrate research into future careers. These findings highlight opportunities for targeted mentorship, greater research autonomy, financial support, and expanded rural training pathways to align resident priorities with workforce needs.

papers.abstract: The solicitation of same-day consent for participation in clinical research is commonly prohibited by research ethics boards because of concerns about limited decision-making time and patient vulnerability. However, these concerns lack empirical support and restrict both research efforts and patient participation opportunities, particularly in medical specialties such as emergency medicine, critical care, and anesthesiology, in which clinicians and patients interact for the first time on the day of a procedure. We aimed to assess the voluntariness of research consent solicited on the day of surgery compared with consent obtained in advance. We performed a prospective, noninferiority randomized controlled trial examining the voluntariness of informed consent to participate in a low-risk clinical research trial at Women's College Hospital in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. The trial design included active deception (invitation to participate in a fabricated research trial) to capture authentic measurements of participants' perceptions of any perceived coercion. We randomized 114 patients scheduled to undergo anterior cruciate ligament repair for recruitment into a fabricated low-risk perioperative research trial at one of two time points: at a virtual preanesthesia clinic appointment in advance of the day of surgery, or on the day of surgery. Regardless of their decision, all participants received the (same) standard of care. Overall, 71/114 patients (62%) either consented to participate in the fabricated trial or declined participation but consented to a feedback session during which perceptions of coercion were assessed. Greater participation was observed among patients approached on the day of surgery (fabricated trial, 26/58 [45%]; feedback session only, 18/58 [31%]) than in advance (fabricated trial, 17/56 [30%]; feedback session only, 10/56 [18%]). Perceived coercion, measured using two validated psychometric instruments, did not differ between patients recruited on the day of surgery and those recruited in advance. A subset of patients in each group reported modest perceptions of undue influence, but regardless of recruitment time point, these patients demonstrated their agency to decline participation. Our findings suggest that restrictive same-day consent policies, when based on concerns regarding undue influence, may represent a structural barrier to participation in low-risk trials that lacks empirical justification. 1) Open Science Framework ( 46twc ); first submitted 17 March 2023; 2) ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT07380035 ); first submitted 16 January 2026.

papers.abstract: Post-ICU care often misses patients unable to attend in-person clinic visits. Remote assessments of physical function might increase access to ICU aftercare. We investigated whether patient-reported disability predicts handgrip strength (HGS) and the 2-Minute Walk Test (2MWT) distance with sufficient clinical accuracy. This secondary analysis of the stepped-wedge cluster-randomised Enhanced Recovery after Intensive Care trial included patients from 10 German ICU clusters who completed the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS) 2.0 plus either HGS, the 2MWT, or both, 6 months after ICU discharge. Relationships between WHODAS 2.0, HGS, and 2MWT were analysed using scatter plots, correlation coefficients, linear regressions, and Bland-Altman plots. Predictions of HGS and the 2MWT were compared with the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for both measures. Of 1463 enrolled patients, 620 were analysed. The median WHODAS 2.0 sum score was 11 (Q1, Q3: 3, 22). The median HGS, expressed as a percentage of the expected value (%exp), was 70.6%exp (Q1, Q3: 54.4, 85.6), and the median 2MWT distance was 73.7%exp (Q1, Q3: 61.5, 85.8). The 2MWT was not completed by 59% of patients. Higher disability was moderately correlated with lower HGS (Spearman %exp: -0.41) and shorter 2MWT distance (Spearman %exp: -0.47). In multivariable regression models, the WHODAS 2.0 sum score predicted HGS in kg (β: -0.27 [95% CI: -0.33 to -0.22]; P<0.001) and 2MWT distance in m (β: -1.94 [95% CI: -2.37 to -1.51]; P<0.001), but the limits of agreement exceeded the MCIDs. With increasing disability, HGS and 2MWT performance declined, although correlations were moderate and uncertainty of predictions exceeded MCIDs of both instruments. Remote WHODAS 2.0 assessments cannot replace in-person physical function testing. NCT03671447.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Interstage infants with single‐ventricle (SV) physiology following Stage I palliation represent a high‐risk population for noncardiac procedures requiring anesthesia. Data comparing perioperative outcomes by shunt type remain limited. Aims Describe anesthetic management, perioperative complications, and postoperative outcomes in interstage SV infants undergoing noncardiac interventions and compare outcomes between right ventricle‐to‐pulmonary artery (Sano) and modified Blalock‐Taussig‐Thomas shunt (mBTTS) patients. Methods We performed a retrospective single‐center cohort study of interstage SV infants with Stage I palliation undergoing noncardiac surgery or nonsurgical procedures requiring anesthesia between 2015 and 2023. Outcomes were stratified by shunt type. Results A total of 208 noncardiac interventions in 120 interstage SV infants were analyzed; 136 (65.4%) encounters in 86 Sano patients and 72 (34.6%) encounters in 34 mBTTS patients. Compared with mBTTS infants, Sano patients underwent interventions at a younger age (57 [IQR 40–83] vs. 105 [59–278] days, p < 0.001) and lower weight (3.6 [3.0–4.1] vs. 4.8 [3.4–7.3] kg, p < 0.001). mBTTS procedures had higher rates of ventricular dysfunction (34.3% vs. 12.7%, p < 0.001), chromosomal abnormalities (63.9% vs. 19.1%, p < 0.001), gastrointestinal comorbidities (87.5% vs. 72.1%, p = 0.014), and hematologic comorbidities (41.7% vs. 22.8%, p = 0.006). Hemodynamic instability requiring vasoactive support was the most common perioperative complication and occurred similarly between groups (31.9% mBTTS vs. 31.6% Sano, p = 0.962). There were no perioperative cardiac arrests. Rates of postoperative escalation of care (2.9%), reintubation (3.0% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.999), readmission (16.2% vs. 16.9%, p = 0.999), and 30‐day mortality (2.3% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.999) were low and comparable between groups. Conclusions Despite the high‐risk physiology of interstage SV patients, perioperative outcomes were comparable between Sano and mBTTS cohorts. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and should not imply low procedural risk. Favorable outcomes likely reflect careful patient selection, multidisciplinary perioperative care, and specialized institutional expertise.

papers.abstract: The erector spinae plane block (ESPB) is widely used for primary breast cancer surgery (BCS), though its clinical benefits within optimized multimodal analgesia pathways remain uncertain. Intravenous lidocaine infusion (IVLI) offers a simple, reproducible alternative with potential systemic analgesic effects. This randomized, tripleblinded, placebo controlled, twocentre trial compared the quality of recovery after ESPB versus IVLI for BCS. Eighty adult patients undergoing primary BCS, with or without axillary dissection, were randomized to receive either ultrasoundguided ESPB (n=40) or intraoperative IVLI (n=40), in addition to a standardized multimodal analgesic protocol. The primary outcome was quality of recovery (QoR15) score at 24 hours. Secondary outcomes included postoperative pain scores, opioid consumption, adverse events, and rescue analgesia requirements. Both interventions produced excellent postoperative recovery, with 24hour QoR15 scores approaching preoperative baselines with no significant difference between groups (mean (SD) 24-hour QoR score; ESPB vs. IVLI group, 137.7(17.9) vs. 136.3(8.8), p=0.61). Pain burden and analgesic requirements over the first 24 hours were similarly low, and no ESPB or lidocainerelated adverse events were observed. Within a standardized multimodal analgesic framework, postoperative recovery and analgesic outcomes did not differ significantly between IVLI and ESPB, suggesting that IVLI may offer a pragmatic alternative when regional anesthesia expertise is limited.

papers.abstract: Recovery after non-cardiac surgery increasingly occurs at home, where clinical deterioration may go unrecognized. Digital health interventions may extend postoperative surveillance beyond discharge, but vary widely in components and clinician involvement. We evaluated their association with readmission and other outcomes. Five databases were searched from inception to December 12, 2025, for prospective randomized and observational studies comparing digital health interventions with standard care in adults after non-cardiac surgery. Readmission was the primary outcome; all-cause and major complications, emergency room (ER) visits, length of stay (LOS), and patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) were secondary. Interventions were grouped by whether a clinician reviewed patient-submitted data and had the ability to take action (active clinician involvement). Random-effects models pooled risk ratios (RR), mean differences (MD), and standardized mean differences (SMD). p values were adjusted for multiple comparisons (Benjamini-Hochberg). In 38 studies (30 randomized, 8 observational; 7,494 patients), digital health interventions were associated with fewer readmissions (17 studies, n=3,944; RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.73-0.99, adjusted p=0.045), ER visits (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.63-0.97), and major complications (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.60-0.94), but not all-cause complications (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.79-1.08) or LOS (MD -0.04 days, 95% CI -0.26 to 0.18). Pain and anxiety were lower and functional status, quality-of-life, and satisfaction scores higher (absolute SMD 0.41-0.69). Readmission risk was lower with active clinician involvement (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.64-0.92) but not without it (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.78-1.18; interaction p=0.029). Heterogeneity in interventions, cohorts, and outcomes was substantial (PROM I² 50-97%). Digital health interventions were associated with fewer readmissions, ER visits, major complications, and better PROMs, but not fewer all-cause complications or shorter LOS. The readmission association was concentrated in studies with active clinician involvement. Heterogeneity was substantial and certainty of evidence low to very low.

papers.abstract: Paratracheal air cysts are rare benign anatomical variants. Although case reports suggest that paratracheal air cysts may lead to complications such as difficult ventilation and pneumothorax in patients whose lungs are mechanically ventilated, their association with postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) remains unclear. We hypothesized that the presence of cysts is associated with an increased incidence of PPCs. In the context of COVID-19, we conducted a retrospective study of all patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia in 2020. On the basis of the presence of paratracheal air cysts, we divided patients into two groups: the paratracheal air cyst group and the paratracheal-air-cyst‑free group. The primary outcome was the incidence of PPCs. We used propensity score matching to adjust for confounding and performed multivariable logistic regression analysis in the matched cohort to assess the association. Among 7,208 patients, the prevalence of paratracheal air cysts was 2.0% (141/7,208). The incidence of PPCs was 22% (31/141) in the paratracheal air cyst group and 15% (43/280) in the paratracheal-air-cyst-free group. Multivariable regression analysis showed that, after adjusting for confounders, the presence of paratracheal air cysts was associated with an increased risk of PPCs (adjusted odds ratio, 1.85; 95% confidence interval, 1.03 to 3.33; P = 0.04). The presence of paratracheal air cysts was associated with an increased risk of PPCs. Although this association warrants cautious interpretation due to possible residual confounding and lack of data on intraoperative ventilatory settings, anesthesiologists should consider the potential perioperative implications of this anatomical abnormality during preoperative assessment.

papers.abstract: Given the fiduciary responsibility of an academic clinical department to ensure appropriate use of funds to support research, the Department of Anesthesia, Pain Management and Perioperative Medicine at Dalhousie University (Halifax, NS, Canada) aimed to create a framework to support the allocation of remunerated protected research time to clinician faculty members within the department. A departmental Research Accountability Project (RAP) was undertaken in the context of a quality improvement initiative. The RAP initially engaged clinician faculty members in the form of a survey, interviews, and a questionnaire to provide feedback regarding current practices for evaluating protected time for research. On the basis of this feedback, a working group created a list of 151 research outputs encompassing the breadth of research-related activities and assigned scores based on their relative merit. Clinicians with protected research time completed their academic profile, and individual point allocations were calculated. Scores were then weighted by different categories (e.g., publications, grant capture, presentations), and a RAP dashboard was developed to capture research outputs, assign scores, and generate a reporting/feedback mechanism for further analysis. Faculty members acknowledged the importance of clinicians having remunerated protected time to carry out research; nevertheless, there was scepticism with respect to how protected research time was managed. These data were then assessed by the working group, and using the RAP metric, individual researcher reports consisting of scores and recommendations were sent to the department head for final evaluation. These reports formed the basis of the researchers' annual academic performance review and consideration for continuance. The RAP scoring system provides an objective measure of remunerated protected research time for clinicians to assist in researcher accountability.

papers.abstract: Predicting difficult intubation is still challenging, even with videolaryngoscopy. Videolaryngoscopy (VL) shows the larynx during intubation. The modified Cormack-Lehane (CL) classification grades laryngeal visibility but can vary between observers. Deep learning uses neural networks for objective, real-time airway image evaluation. We aimed to evaluate a YOLOv8-based model for object detection to automate modified CL grade classification from VL images in patients undergoing elective surgery. In this prospective observational study, we developed a deep learning model using 346 VL images from 151 patients undergoing elective surgery. Two anesthesiologists classified images according to the modified CL system, and interobserver agreement was analysed using Cohen's kappa and weighted kappa. We split the data into training (80%), validation (10%), and test (10%) sets, with imbalance corrected via Albumentations augmentation. We evaluated the model results using sensitivity, specificity, and mean average precision with a 95% confidence interval (CI) and validated the model on 60 images not included in the training set. Interobserver agreement ranged from moderate (Cohen's kappa = 0.59; 95% CI, 0.53 to 0.66) to good (weighted kappa = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.75 to 0.84). In the test set, the overall recall rate was 0.87, and the specificity was 0.83. In the difficult intubation grades, recall and specificity were observed to be 0.79 (95% CI, 0.52 to 0.92) and 0.93 (95% CI, 0.78 to 0.98), respectively, for CL grade 2b, and 0.60 and 1.00, respectively, for CL grade 3. In the external validation data set (n = 60), the model achieved an overall accuracy of 0.767 with a recognition rate of 0.925 for clinically relevant CL grades 2b and 3. The YOLOv8-based model showed promising performance in classifying modified CL grades, particularly for clinically relevant difficult views (CL grades 2b-3). Nevertheless, wide CIs and limited external validation indicate uncertainty. The model may be considered an auxiliary tool rather than an independent decision system and requires further validation in larger, multicentre data sets.

papers.abstract: Summary Introduction Difficult tracheal intubation is associated with serious complications, including hypoxia, bradycardia and cardiac arrest. Neonates have increased physiologic vulnerability compared with older children, yet detailed data on management strategies and outcomes in neonates with difficult tracheal intubation remain limited. We hypothesised that clinicians have lower first‐attempt tracheal intubation success and higher complication rates for neonates compared with older children with difficult tracheal intubation. Methods We analysed the Pediatric Difficult Intubation Registry to determine tracheal intubation first attempt success and incidence of complications. We used logistic regression to identify variables associated with complications in neonates. Results During the study period, 6283 paediatric difficult tracheal intubations were recorded, including 420 neonates. First attempt success was lower for neonates (139/420, 33.1%) than older children (2394/4683, 51.1%). Complications occurred more frequently in neonates (123/420, 29.3%) than older children (637/4683, 13.6%). Hypoxia occurred in 92/420 (21.9%) neonates and 269/4683 (5.7%) older children. Severe complications were more frequent in neonates vs. older children (12/420, 2.9% vs. 30/4683, 0.6%, respectively), with cardiac arrests occurring in 4/420 (1.0%) neonates and 11/4683 (0.2%) older children. Difficult mask ventilation occurred more frequently in neonates (60/420, 14.3%) than older children (353/4681, 7.5%). In neonates, increased number of tracheal intubation attempts (aOR 1.61 per attempt, 95%CI 1.30–2.00, p < 0.001) and difficult facemask ventilation (aOR 3.17, 95%CI 1.38–7.30, p = 0.007) were associated with complications. Anticipated difficulty with airway management had a protective effect (aOR 0.37, 95%CI 0.16–0.88, p = 0.025). Discussion Neonates with difficult tracheal intubation experience a substantially higher rate of complications than older children. Early recognition of risk is critical in order to enable careful planning to minimise tracheal intubation attempts in this vulnerable population.
